claim: Biomolecular condensates are formed by liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS) of multivalent molecules.
source: Biomolecular condensates are formed by liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS) of multivalent molecules.
evidence: This is a foundational statement in the abstract that is supported by the established scientific literature cited throughout the manuscript.

claim: LLPS from a single (homotypic) constituent is governed by buffering: above a threshold, free monomer concentration is clamped, with all added molecules entering the condensed phase.
source: LLPS from a single ("homotypic") constituent is governed by buffering: above a threshold, free monomer concentration is clamped, with all added molecules entering the condensed phase.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations in the introduction and is a well-established principle in the field.

claim: Buffering fails for the concentration dependence of multicomponent (heterotypic) LLPS.
source: However, both experiment and theory demonstrate that buffering fails for the concentration dependence of multicomponent ("heterotypic") LLPS.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental and theoretical studies cited in the manuscript, particularly Riback et al., 2020 and Choi et al., 2019.

claim: The product of free monomer concentrations, accounting for ideal stoichiometries governed by valencies, displays a threshold above which additional monomers are funneled into large clusters.
source: Using network-free stochastic modeling, we demonstrate that LLPS can be described by the solubility product constant (Ksp): the product of free monomer concentrations, accounting for the ideal stoichiometries governed by the valencies, displays a threshold above which additional monomers are funneled into large clusters
evidence: This claim is supported by the simulation data presented in the manuscript, particularly Figures 1-7.

claim: The Ksp concept reduces to simple buffering for homotypic systems.
source: this reduces to simple buffering for homotypic systems.
evidence: This is demonstrated through the modeling results and is consistent with established knowledge about homotypic systems.

claim: The Ksp regulates the composition of the dilute phase for a wide range of valencies and stoichiometries.
source: The Ksp regulates the composition of the dilute phase for a wide range of valencies and stoichiometries.
evidence: This is supported by simulation data across multiple scenarios with varying valencies and stoichiometries presented in Figures 3-6.

claim: Coarse-grained spatial particle simulations support the role of Ksp.
source: The role of Ksp is further supported by coarse-grained spatial particle simulations.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the SpringSaLaD simulation results presented in Figure 7.

claim: Biomolecular condensates serve as membraneless compartments where complex biochemistry can be organized and facilitated.
source: These structures serve as membraneless compartments where complex biochemistry can be organized and facilitated (Holehouse and Pappu, 2018)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Holehouse and Pappu, 2018.

claim: T cell receptor-mediated actin nucleation efficacy increases multifold when associated signaling molecules concentrate into a condensate near the plasma membrane.
source: for example, T cell receptor-mediated actin nucleation efficacy spikes up multifold when all the associated signaling molecules concentrate into a condensate (Su et al., 2016) near the plasma membrane.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Su et al., 2016.

claim: Biomolecular condensates are implicated in many age-related or neurological diseases.
source: These structures are also implicated in many age-related or neurological diseases (Shin and Brangwynne, 2017; Alberti et al., 2019; Mathieu et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Shin and Brangwynne, 2017; Alberti et al., 2019; Mathieu et al., 2020.

claim: Clustering of weakly interacting multivalent proteins or nucleic acids is a prerequisite for phase separation.
source: In particular, it is firmly established that clustering of weakly interacting multivalent proteins or nucleic acids is a prerequisite for the phase separation.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Li et al., 2012; Shin et al., 2017; Wang et al., 2018.

claim: A sufficiently concentrated solution of a single self-interacting protein with multiple binding sites can partition into protein-dense and dilute phases.
source: Even a sufficiently concentrated solution of a single self-interacting protein (homotypic interaction) with multiple binding sites in its sequence can partition into protein-dense and dilute phases.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field supported by the cited literature.

claim: Homotypic phase separation serves as a buffering mechanism for the protein in the dilute phase.
source: Such homotypic systems display a strict threshold concentration above which phase separation occurs. This phase separation serves as a buffering mechanism for the protein in the dilute phase (Holehouse and Pappu, 2018; Klosin et al., 2020), which remains at the threshold concentration
evidence: This is supported by citations to Holehouse and Pappu, 2018; Klosin et al., 2020.

claim: In homotypic systems, as more protein is added, the dense phase droplets grow in size and number, keeping the concentration clamped in the dilute phase.
source: thus, as more protein is added to the system, the dense phase droplets grow in size and number, keeping the concentration clamped in the dilute phase.
evidence: This is established knowledge about homotypic systems supported by the cited literature.

claim: Dilute phase concentrations of specific components in heterotypic systems need not stay fixed when phase separation is driven by heterotypic interactions.
source: Detailed theoretical analysis of lattice-based simulations explained why the dilute phase concentrations of specific components need not stay fixed when phase separation is driven by heterotypic interactions (Choi et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Choi et al., 2019.

claim: Concentration thresholds for phase separation in heterotypic systems vary with relative compositions of interacting binding partners.
source: This was recently followed by a thorough experimental study of the thermodynamics of the liquid-liquid phase transitions in heterotypic systems, showing clearly that concentration thresholds for phase separation no longer remain fixed and vary with relative compositions of interacting binding partners (Riback et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Riback et al., 2020.

claim: A theoretical framework for quantitatively predicting complex varying concentration thresholds in heterotypic systems is lacking.
source: But a theoretical framework for quantitatively predicting such complex varying concentration thresholds is still lacking.
evidence: This statement identifies a gap in the literature that the current work aims to address.

claim: Strong multivalent interactions can produce molecular machines with fixed stoichiometry.
source: We have previously distinguished between strong multivalent interactions, which can produce molecular machines, and weak multivalent interactions, which can produce what we termed 'pleomorphic ensembles' (Mayer et al., 2009; Falkenberg et al., 2013). The strong binding affinities in molecular machines (e.g., ribosomes, flagella) enforce a specific parts list with a fixed stoichiometry.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Mayer et al., 2009; Falkenberg et al., 2013.

claim: Pleomorphic ensembles are more plastic in their composition than molecular machines.
source: Pleomorphic ensembles (e.g., cytoskeletal polymers and their associated binding proteins, neuronal post-synaptic densities, etc.) are much more plastic in their composition than molecular machines.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Mayer et al., 2009; Falkenberg et al., 2013.

claim: Biomolecular condensates are a subclass of pleomorphic ensembles.
source: Biomolecular condensates are a subclass of pleomorphic ensembles in that their molecular components simultaneously coexist within both a distinct phase and as solutes in the surrounding solution.
evidence: This is a conceptual classification based on the properties of biomolecular condensates.

claim: For AgCl, Ksp = 1.7 × 10−10 M2 at 25°C.
source: For AgCl Ksp = 1.7 × 10−10 M2 at 25°C.
evidence: This is established knowledge from solution chemistry.

claim: Adding Cl- in the form of a highly soluble salt into an AgCl solution will cause some AgCl to precipitate to maintain the solubility product at Ksp.
source: Importantly, if we add any Cl- in the form of a highly soluble salt (e.g., KCl) into the solution, some AgCl will precipitate to maintain the solubility product at Ksp.
evidence: This is established knowledge from solution chemistry (common ion effect).

claim: For a tetravalent heterotypic pair (A4 and B4) with Kd of 350 µM, the Ksp is 169 µM2.
source: upon reaching a concentration threshold (total concentration ~120 µM in this case), SP plateaus to a constant value (169 µM2). This is the solubility product constant or Ksp for this pair of tetravalent molecules.
evidence: This is directly measured from the simulation data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Below the Ksp threshold, the cluster size distribution is insensitive to the number of molecules at a given total concentration.
source: If the system shows no tendency to condense into large clusters, the size distribution will be insensitive to the number of molecules at a given total concentration. Figure 1B shows this to be the case for the 80 µM total concentration (SP = 154 µM2 < Ksp).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the simulation data in Figure 1B.

claim: Below Ksp, approximately 80% of total molecules are in clusters containing less than 10 molecules, regardless of the number of molecules in the system.
source: Approximately 80% of the total molecules are in clusters containing less than 10 molecules, no matter how many molecules are available in the system.
evidence: This is quantified from the simulation data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Above the Ksp threshold, the cluster size distribution becomes bimodal and extends to larger clusters as more molecules are added.
source: The histogram does change shape, extending the tail to larger clusters eventually to become a bimodal distribution as we feed more molecules into the system (i.e., as we increase the volume).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the simulation data in Figure 1C.

claim: With 1600 molecules at 160 µM total concentration (above Ksp), more than 20% of total molecules are in clusters larger than 100 molecules.
source: With 1600 molecules in the system, more than 20% of the total molecules are in clusters larger than 100 molecules.
evidence: This is quantified from the simulation data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Individual trajectories above Ksp show almost all molecules in one huge cluster along with small oligomers.
source: examination of individual histograms in Figure 1—figure supplement 3 (note the logarithmic scale on the abscissa) shows almost all of them individually containing just one huge cluster along with small oligomers.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the individual trajectory data in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: A constant solubility product (Ksp) is a quantitative indicator to mark the threshold that underlies biomolecular condensates.
source: We hypothesize that this tendency to form increasingly larger clusters with more available molecules is a hallmark of phase separation behavior, as previously established (Chattaraj et al., 2019), and that a constant solubility product (Ksp) is a quantitative indicator to mark the threshold that underlies biomolecular condensates.
evidence: This is the central hypothesis of the paper, supported by the simulation data presented.

claim: Below the threshold where SP has not reached Ksp, the system exists as a single phase with low tendency to form large clusters.
source: Below a threshold total concentration, when SP has not reached the constant level of Ksp, the tendency to form large clusters is low and the system would exist as a single phase (e.g., Figure 1B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the simulation data in Figure 1B.

claim: Above the threshold where SP converges to Ksp, the system forms very large clusters yielding two different phases.
source: Above the threshold where SP converges to the Ksp, the system tends to form very large clusters, yielding two different phases, manifest as bimodal cluster size histograms (Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 2B, and Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the simulation data in Figure 1C and supplementary figures.

claim: For CMC at 12.9 µM (SP = 166.4 µM2, below Ksp), total molecular concentrations converge to a steady state of approximately 56 µM.
source: For CMC_A4 = CMC_B4 = 12.9 µM (SP = 166.4 µM2, below Ksp), total molecular concentrations rise up initially and then converge to a steady state (~56 µM) (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the CMC simulation data in Figure 2B.

claim: At CMC = 13 µM (SP = 169 µM2 = Ksp), the total concentrations never reach a steady state.
source: However, going to CMC = 13 µM (SP = 169 µM2 = Ksp), the total concentrations never reach a steady state.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the CMC simulation data in Figure 2B.

claim: At CMC = 13 µM (at Ksp), the system shows large fluctuations and variable lag times before irreversible growth.
source: When we look at the individual trajectories (Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplements 1–3), the system shows large fluctuations and variable lag times before irreversible growth near the phase boundary (Figure 2C, CMC = 13 µM)
evidence: This is demonstrated by the individual trajectory data in Figure 2C and supplementary figures.

claim: The behavior at Ksp represents stochastic nucleation of clusters containing enough crosslinking that disassembly becomes unlikely.
source: The behavior at Ksp represents stochastic nucleation of clusters containing enough crosslinking that disassembly becomes unlikely; such larger clusters are sufficiently stable only at or above Ksp.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the simulation data showing stochastic behavior at Ksp.

claim: Below the phase boundary, clamping monomer concentrations to values from the FTC method recovers the same steady-state total molecular concentrations in the CMC method.
source: Below the phase boundary, if we clamp the monomer concentrations to the value of free concentrations obtained from the FTC method, we recover the same steady-state total molecular concentrations (top six panels in Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the comparison data in Figure 2—figure supplement 4.

claim: Above Ksp, the CMC total concentration increases with time rather than leveling off to a steady value.
source: However, at even slightly above the Ksp, the CMC total concentration increases with time, rather than leveling off to a higher steady value (bottom panels in Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the comparison data in Figure 2—figure supplement 4.

claim: For SP < Ksp, systems with varying individual CMCs converge to stable steady states regardless of individual monomer concentrations.
source: Satisfyingly, we find that for SP < Ksp (Figure 3B), the systems converge to stable steady states (no phase transition)
evidence: This is demonstrated by the simulation data in Figure 3B.

claim: For SP > Ksp, systems always show unbounded growth (phase transition) irrespective of individual clamped concentrations.
source: but for SP > Ksp (Figure 3A), irrespective of individual clamped concentrations, systems always show unbounded growth (phase transition).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the simulation data in Figure 3A.

claim: When A4 and B4 are titrated at a 3:2 ratio, the free monomer concentration of the lower abundant component (B4) gets exhausted disproportionately as the threshold is approached.
source: Interestingly, in this computational experiment the free monomer concentration of the lower abundant component (B4) gets exhausted disproportionately as the threshold is approached, so that SP cannot quite reach Ksp (169 µM2) and actually begins to diminish somewhat at still higher FTC.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the simulation data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Even when monomer supply becomes depleted, the Ksp still serves as an upper limit for free monomer concentrations.
source: Thus, even when monomer supply becomes depleted, the Ksp still serves as an upper limit for free monomer concentrations.
evidence: This is inferred from the simulation data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Increasing valency increases the propensity for phase separation.
source: Increasing valency is known to increase the propensity for phase separation (Holehouse and Pappu, 2018; Mathieu et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Holehouse and Pappu, 2018; Mathieu et al., 2020.

claim: The total concentration needed to reach Ksp decreases with higher valency.
source: The total concentration needed to reach the Ksp goes down with higher valency, consistent with experiment.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the simulation data in Figure 4.

claim: Going from a 3v,3v pair to a 4v,4v pair, Ksp changes over fivefold (852 µM2 to 169 µM2).
source: Going from 3v,3v pair to 4v,4v pair, Ksp changes over fivefold (852 µM2 to 169 µM2)
evidence: This is quantified from the simulation data in Figure 4.

claim: Going from a 4v,4v pair to a 5v,5v pair, Ksp changes approximately threefold (169 µM2 to 55 µM2).
source: whereas approximately threefold change (169 µM2 to 55 µM2) can be observed for transitioning into 5v,5v pair from 4v,4v.
evidence: This is quantified from the simulation data in Figure 4.

claim: For a mixed-valent A5-B3 system at 3A5:5B3 stoichiometry, the free monomer concentration of B3 goes up steadily while free A5 goes up first and then starts to go down.
source: Maintaining this concentration ratio, as we titrate up the total concentrations, we see an interesting pattern (Figure 5A, inset): the free monomer concentration of B3, which is present in excess, goes up steadily; but the free A5 goes up first and then starts to go down.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the simulation data in Figure 5A inset.

claim: For the A5-B3 mixed-valent system, the simple product of free monomer concentrations does not plateau to a constant Ksp.
source: When we take the product of free monomer concentrations (Figure 5—figure supplement 1), we do not see an SP profile that plateaus to a constant Ksp (as in Figure 1A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the simulation data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: For the A5-B3 system, when SP is corrected by ideal stoichiometry as SP = (free A5)3(free B3)5, the SP profile plateaus to a fixed Ksp beyond the total concentration threshold of ~128 μM.
source: However, when we correct the SP expression by taking the ideal stoichiometry into account, SP = (free A5)3(free B3)5, we get an SP profile that does plateau to a fixed Ksp beyond the total concentration threshold of ~128 μM (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the simulation data in Figure 5A.

claim: For the A5-B3 mixed-valent system, the free monomer concentrations do not display buffering above the threshold.
source: Importantly, the free monomer concentrations do not display buffering above this threshold (Figure 5A, inset), with the concentration of the pentavalent monomer actually decreasing.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the simulation data in Figure 5A inset.

claim: The Ksp analogy between ionic solution chemistry and biomolecular condensates holds for complex stoichiometries.
source: Thus, the Ksp analogy between ionic solution chemistry and biomolecular condensates seems to hold for even these more complex stoichiometries.
evidence: This is inferred from the simulation results for mixed-valent systems.

claim: Simple multivalent binding simulations can reproduce experimental titration patterns showing that components of heterotypic biomolecular condensates are not effectively buffered in the dilute phase.
source: The simulation results in Figure 6 show that our simple multivalent binding system is able to reproduce these experimental titration patterns
evidence: This is demonstrated by comparing simulation data in Figure 6 with experimental data from Riback et al., 2020.

claim: Despite failure of simple buffering in heterotypic systems, concentrations of individual components in the dilute phase are still constrained by Ksp.
source: importantly, it also further demonstrates, despite this failure of simple buffering, that the concentrations of individual components in the dilute phase are still constrained by Ksp.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the simulation data in Figure 6D.

claim: For the ternary A3-B1,3-C6 system, the Ksp is approximately 1012 µM11.
source: Both of these titrations plateau to the same value of Ksp of ~1012 µM11
evidence: This is quantified from the simulation data in Figure 6D.

claim: For the ternary system, individual monomer concentrations continue to change dramatically even after the Ksp is reached.
source: Figure 6—figure supplement 3A also shows how the individual monomer concentrations (insets) continue to change dramatically even after the Ksp is reached.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the simulation data in Figure 6—figure supplement 3A.

claim: For the spatial tetravalent A4a-B4b system, the SP converges to a constant value (Ksp = 318 µM2) at a threshold FTC of approximately 138 µM.
source: The SP converges to a constant value (Ksp = 318 µM2) at a threshold FTC (~138 µM in this case).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the SpringSaLaD simulation data in Figure 7B.

claim: In spatial simulations of the A4a-B4b system, the dimer emerges as a preferred configuration both below and above Ksp.
source: When we look at the detailed cluster size distributions at steady state (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A), the dimer emerges as a preferred configuration both below and above the Ksp.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the SpringSaLaD simulation data in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The dimer preference in spatial simulations arises from the matching valency and spatial arrangement of binding sites, an effect termed 'dimer trap' that cannot be realized in non-spatial methods.
source: This dimer preference arises from the matching valency and spatial arrangement of the binding sites in the two partner molecules; such an effect, which we term a 'dimer trap,' cannot be realized in non-spatial methods, such as NFsim.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the spatial simulation results explaining the difference from non-spatial simulations.

claim: In spatial simulations above Ksp, most individual trajectories produce discontinuous distributions with small oligomers along with one or two very large clusters.
source: Above Ksp, however, most of the individual trajectories, much like NFsim, produce discontinuous distributions with small oligomers along with one or two very larger clusters (Figure 7—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the SpringSaLaD simulation data in Figure 7—figure supplement 2.

claim: For spatial simulations with CMC below Ksp (16.7 µM), total concentrations converge to a steady state.
source: Below that boundary (CMC = 16.7 µM), total concentrations converge to a steady state (Figure 7C, top panel)
evidence: This is demonstrated by the SpringSaLaD CMC simulation data in Figure 7C.

claim: For spatial simulations with CMC at or above Ksp (17.85 µM or 18 µM), the total concentration of molecules keeps increasing with time.
source: at (CMC = 17.85 µM) or above the boundary (CMC = 18 µM), the total concentration of molecules keeps on going up with time (Figure 7C, second and third panels).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the SpringSaLaD CMC simulation data in Figure 7C.

claim: Stochastic fluctuations are somewhat greater in spatial simulations than in non-spatial scenarios.
source: As quantified by the error bars (Figure 7C, second and third panels), stochastic fluctuations are somewhat greater in spatial simulations than the non-spatial scenario.
evidence: This is observed by comparing error bars in spatial vs. non-spatial simulation results.

claim: Higher variability in spatial simulations is expected due to a larger number of contributing factors like steric crowding and optimal geometric conformations of binding sites.
source: This stochasticity can be attributed to the variable lag before the nucleation of a sufficiently large cluster for irreversible and accelerating growth; higher variability in spatial simulations is expected due to a larger number of contributing factors like steric crowding and optimal geometric conformations of binding sites.
evidence: This is an interpretation explaining the observed differences between spatial and non-spatial simulations.

claim: The Ksp concept remains valid for the spatial system shown in Figure 7A.
source: Thus, the Ksp concept remains valid for the spatial system shown in Figure 7A.
evidence: This is concluded from the SpringSaLaD simulation results in Figure 7.

claim: For most scenarios, the Ksp defines a threshold for unbounded growth of large clusters and a quantitative metric for the tendency of a system to phase separate.
source: We found that for most scenarios, if not all, the Ksp does define a threshold for the unbounded growth of large clusters and a quantitative metric for the tendency of a system to phase separate.
evidence: This is the main conclusion from the computational modeling results.

claim: Experimental systems may introduce additional levels of complexity such as nonspecific low-affinity binding interactions and long-range electrostatic forces.
source: But it is important to appreciate that experimental systems may introduce additional levels of complexity, such as nonspecific low-affinity binding interactions and long-range electrostatic forces.
evidence: This is a caveat acknowledging limitations of the simplified models.

claim: For real biomolecular condensates, the valency and stoichiometry of components may be unknown, and they may have multiple binding interactions of differing affinities.
source: For real biomolecular condensates, the valency and stoichiometry of the components may be unknown, and they may have multiple binding interaction of differing affinities.
evidence: This acknowledges the complexity of real biological systems compared to the simplified models.

claim: It should be possible to measure Ksp experimentally using fluorescently labeled binding partners and determining their concentrations in dilute and condensed phases via quantitative confocal microscopy.
source: However, it should be possible to measure Ksp experimentally using fluorescently labeled binding partners and determining their concentrations in the dilute and condensed phase via quantitative confocal microscopy (Fink et al., 1998).
evidence: This is a proposed experimental approach supported by citation to Fink et al., 1998.

claim: Titration experiments can readily be performed in vitro and have been among the earliest studies of biomolecular condensates.
source: Titration experiments can readily be performed in vitro and have been among the earliest studies of biomolecular condensates (Li et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Li et al., 2012.

claim: Methods have been developed to perform titrations in cells.
source: More recently, methods have been developed to perform titrations in cells (Riback et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Riback et al., 2020.

claim: Experimental data on Ksp could provide an indication of the effective valency of interactions in complex multivalent biomolecular condensates.
source: Beyond validation, enough such data may make it possible to find optimal fits to a Ksp expression, providing an indication of the effective valency of the interactions in complex multivalent biomolecular condensates.
evidence: This is a proposed application of the Ksp concept to experimental data.

claim: NFsim is a non-spatial rule-based stochastic simulation framework where each biomolecule represents a molecular object that may have multiple binding sites.
source: To develop models that probe for the effects of valency and concentrations but do not account for spatial effects, we employ the NFsim (Sneddon et al., 2011) – a non-spatial rule-based stochastic simulation framework where each biomolecule represents a molecular object that may have multiple binding sites.
evidence: This describes the computational method used, supported by citation to Sneddon et al., 2011.

claim: SpringSaLaD is a particle-based spatial simulation platform where each biomolecule is modeled as a collection of hard spheres connected by stiff spring-like linkers.
source: To account for realistic spatial geometry, we employ SringSaLaD (Michalski and Loew, 2016) – a particle-based spatial simulation platform where each biomolecule is modeled as a collection of hard spheres connected by stiff spring-like linkers.
evidence: This describes the computational method used, supported by citation to Michalski and Loew, 2016.

claim: The percolation boundary is generally considered a proxy for phase separation.
source: This bifurcation between one large cluster and small oligomers has been used to define a percolation boundary, generally considered a proxy for phase separation (Choi et al., 2019; Choi et al., 2020a).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Choi et al., 2019; Choi et al., 2020a.

claim: The percolation boundary and phase separation may not be completely coincident.
source: Here, we use the percolation boundary, the threshold for forming large clusters, as a proxy for phase separation, realizing that they may not be completely coincident (Choi et al., 2020a; Choi et al., 2020b).
evidence: This is a caveat supported by citations to Choi et al., 2020a; Choi et al., 2020b.

claim: Buffering of dilute phase concentrations in multicomponent systems has a complex relationship with the interplay of homotypic and heterotypic interactions.
source: Recent computational (Choi et al., 2019) and theoretical (Deviri and Safran, 2021) studies demonstrated that buffering of dilute phase concentrations in multicomponent systems has a complex relationship with the interplay of homotypic and heterotypic interactions.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Choi et al., 2019 and Deviri and Safran, 2021.

claim: For a two-component heterotypic system, the phase diagram has an elliptical region corresponding to coexistence of dilute and condensed phases.
source: For a two-component heterotypic system, plotting the total concentrations of one component against the other produces a phase diagram with an elliptical region corresponding to the coexistence of the dilute and condensed phases
evidence: This is based on theoretical work cited in the manuscript.

claim: In two-component systems, dilute and condensed phase concentrations remain constant (buffered) along tie lines approximately parallel to the major axis of the phase diagram ellipse.
source: In fact, the dilute and condensed phase concentrations remain constant (i.e., buffered) along tie lines that are approximately parallel to the major axis of the ellipse
evidence: This is based on theoretical work by Deviri and Safran, 2021.

claim: Buffering fails perpendicular to tie lines in the phase diagram.
source: buffering fails perpendicular to tie lines (Deviri and Safran, 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Deviri and Safran, 2021.

claim: The SP should be approximately constant (Ksp) within the two-phase elliptic region of the phase diagram.
source: However, the SP should be approximately constant (Ksp) within the two-phase elliptic region.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the Ksp concept applied to phase diagrams.

claim: The SP may be used to predict concentrations in the dilute phase even for short traversals perpendicular to tie lines in the phase diagram.
source: That is, the SP may be used to predict concentrations in the dilute phase even for short traversals perpendicular to tie lines in the phase diagram.
evidence: This is a proposed application of the Ksp concept to phase diagrams.
